lines.text: Hi, Mr. Evans. Thanks for seeing me. I wanted to ask about my schedule for next semester.
Of course. What seems to be the problem?
I'm registered for biology and statistics, but both are on Tuesday and Thursday mornings, and the labs overlap by thirty minutes.
Ah, that happens sometimes. Have you checked whether another section of statistics is open?
I did. There's an evening section, but I work at the library until six on those days.
I see. Well, biology has a Friday lab section as well. If you switch to that, there's no overlap, and your work hours stay the same.
Oh, I didn't know about the Friday lab. Is there still space?
I think so, but it fills up fast. I'd register today if I were you.

ctx: A biology professor gives a short lecture.

lines.text: Let's begin with a simple question: what happens to an ecosystem if one animal disappears? Sometimes, very little. But for a small group of animals, called keystone species, the effects are huge. The sea otter is a classic example. Sea otters eat sea urchins, and sea urchins eat kelp. When hunters nearly wiped out sea otters along the Pacific coast, the urchin population exploded. The urchins grazed down the kelp forests until only bare rock remained. And remember, kelp forests are not just plants. They shelter fish, crabs, and many other species. So, losing the otters meant losing the habitat for dozens of animals. Interestingly, when conservation programs brought the otters back, the kelp began to recover. Notice that sea otters are not the most numerous animals in this ecosystem. A keystone species matters because of what it does, not because of how many there are. For next class, think of another ecosystem where one species might play this role.

ctx: A psychology professor gives a short lecture.

lines.text: Many students believe the best way to prepare for an exam is to study one subject for hours the night before. Psychologists call this massed practice, and it feels productive, because the material seems familiar. But research on memory has shown a better method, called the spacing effect. In one classic experiment, two groups learned the same list of vocabulary words. One group studied for three hours in a single day. The other studied for one hour on three separate days. A week later, the second group remembered significantly more words. Why? Researchers suggest that when you return to material after a break, you have to work to recall it, and that effort strengthens the memory. So cramming may help you pass tomorrow's quiz, but it doesn't help you remember the material next month. That said, spacing takes planning. You can't start the day before the exam. So, if you have a test in two weeks, start now and review in short sessions.

ctx: An environmental science professor gives a short lecture.

lines.text: Have you ever noticed that a city can feel several degrees hotter than the countryside around it? Scientists call this the urban heat island effect. It happens mainly for two reasons. First, materials like asphalt and concrete absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night, so cities don't cool down as quickly. Second, cities have fewer trees and less open ground, and plants help cool the air by releasing water vapor. In some large cities, nighttime temperatures can be as much as five degrees higher than in nearby rural areas. This is more than a comfort issue. Higher temperatures increase electricity use for air conditioning and can be dangerous for older people. So planners are experimenting with solutions, such as painting roofs white to reflect sunlight and planting trees along streets. Next time, we'll look at how well these solutions actually work.

ctx: A history professor gives a short lecture.

lines.text: Before the fifteenth century, every book in Europe was copied by hand, usually by monks. A single book could take months to produce, so books were rare and expensive. Then Johannes Gutenberg introduced a printing press with movable metal letters. The key idea was simple: letters could be rearranged and reused for different pages. Printing became faster and cheaper, and the number of books increased dramatically. What's interesting is the effect this had on ideas. When more people could read the same text, new ideas could spread across countries within years rather than decades. Scholars could also compare printed copies and notice errors, which helped knowledge become more reliable. Of course, this didn't happen overnight. Literacy rates grew slowly, and many people still couldn't afford books. But the press set a pattern we recognize today: when information becomes cheaper to share, society changes.

ctx: A psychology professor gives a short lecture.

lines.text: Imagine you're shopping for a jacket, and the first price you see is three hundred dollars. Later you find a similar jacket for one hundred fifty. Suddenly, the second jacket looks like a bargain, even if one hundred fifty is more than you'd normally pay. This is called anchoring: our judgments are strongly influenced by the first piece of information we receive, even when that information is irrelevant. In a well-known study, participants watched a wheel spin to a random number, then estimated the percentage of African countries in the United Nations. Those who saw a high number gave higher estimates than those who saw a low number, though the wheel had nothing to do with the question. Notice that participants knew the number was random. Even so, it shaped their answers. Marketers use this all the time. A high original price crossed out beside a sale price creates an anchor. The lesson isn't that we should distrust every number. It's that we should ask ourselves where our first impression came from before we decide.
